codex.worst_flaw: The decision to repeat the reward rests on an uncontrolled follow-up, so the programme could repeat it even if the randomized comparison shows no added benefit.

claude.worst_flaw: The keep, change or drop thresholds compare each team only with its own earlier baseline, not with a control group, and the design gives no sample-size or uncertainty plan. It also never specifies versioned, replayable event records, so the persistence decision and any audit rest on weak evidence.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, a staggered lottery rollout, privacy protections and safeguards against box-ticking and unsafe pressure make it approvable, but it is complex to explain, 30 minutes of paid time off is a modest reward, and the follow-up depends on the app fixes rather than the reward to keep the habit going.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot leaves a safety-critical gap by failing to specify how crews prevent work from starting when a required checklist is missed outside an approved outage exception.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no clear way to stop rushed tick-box checklists. Its quality check is a vague 'routine audit' with no sample size, no timing test against GPS or dispatch, and only a falsification trigger, which leaves low-quality but technically valid submissions mostly unpoliced in a safety-critical setting.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, union-involved, safety-conscious pilot with a randomized stepped rollout and fixes to real barriers, but 30 minutes of paid time off may feel modest, the 90% threshold is demanding, and the audit-based verification relies on a single overstretched safety lead.

claude.worst_flaw: The design leaves audit and operations thin. It has no replayable event or policy versioning, no independent shadow validation of the automated count and no staffed appeal process with response times. The 80% target and the staggered comparison also lack a pre-set sample size, a definition of a meaningful lift, and a plan for handling spillover between teams.

codex.worst_flaw: The weekly audit samples only credited jobs, so it can miss cases where technicians were discouraged from recording a safety hold and the job earned no credit.

holistic.reason: Union-consulted, safety-hold-protected, staggered-randomized design with fixes retained after rewards end and clear pause triggers is approvable, though one hour of time off is a modest incentive and the counting and sync rules add complexity for technicians to notice and trust.

claude.worst_flaw: Measurement and appeals rest on one rotation lead reviewing a five-item sample, with no versioned event history, independent shadow validation or permissions. The 'specific change request' and 'documented blocker' credit rules are also left open to light gaming, such as nitpick-only change requests, and to assigning easy reviews to a favoured person.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot sets no decision rule for whether paid time off improves review timeliness enough to justify its cost and any quality trade-offs over queue fixes and private feedback alone.

holistic.reason: Fixing the real bottleneck (protected time, ownership, oldest-first queue) with a small optional reward, anti-gaming checks, and defaults that persist should suit sceptical engineers, though the design is intricate and one hour of PTO is a modest hook.

codex.worst_flaw: The paid-time-off pilot is not launchable as written because submission records establish timeliness, while the five-review spot check leaves the usefulness of most reviews unverified for individual payouts.

claude.worst_flaw: The design cannot separate the reward's effect from the workflow fixes: the comparison uses only two randomized rotations, it sets no cost, harm or quality outcomes in advance, and it tracks no review quality or draft-holding after payouts end. It also pays with paid time off, which removes reviewer capacity, a trade-off the design never addresses.

holistic.reason: Fixes the real bottleneck (routing, protected time, backup, oldest-first) with sensible quality checks and an honest evaluation plan, but a half-day PTO prize for sceptical engineers risks being seen as gamification, and the 25-person sample plus quality-gaming risk make results fragile.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never sets a baseline or success criterion for the reward pilot's net added value. With 25 engineers split by lot, the comparison is only directional, and no decision rule says when to drop the reward. Event and policy versioning and the appeal route are also only thinly specified.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot leaves cross-group reviews unattributed and sets no threshold for how much the reward must improve response times to justify its cost.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, workflow-first and sceptic-friendly with private feedback, a time-off reward, an owner audit and fallback rules, but the 25-minute daily slot and a one-hour reward are modest, the owner's one-hour budget is tight, and the reward ending at week six leaves lasting change dependent on the workflow defaults sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: Launching the kiosk and feedback together on all three wards leaves no comparison that can isolate the kiosk’s effect on hand-hygiene compliance.

claude.worst_flaw: The evaluation is a three-ward before/after check against noisy, small-sample monthly audits, with no concurrent comparison, minimum sample size or account of observer effects. It cannot tell whether the kiosk added anything beyond the access fixes, and the purpose and validity of kiosk logging itself are left undefined.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, safety-conscious and avoids gaming risks with clear stop rules and audit-based measures, but it is low-salience with no tangible reward, so uptake and post-pilot persistence depend on kiosk becoming the default workflow.

codex.worst_flaw: The retention rule can keep the kiosk when audited compliance stays flat even though the pilot never checks whether nurses reliably log eligible hand-hygiene moments.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never defines which hand-hygiene moments nurses should log or how kiosk entries reconcile with observed opportunities, so the logging behaviour and its link to audited compliance remain unspecified and unvalidated.

holistic.reason: It is a careful, low-risk design that avoids rewarding easy-to-count entries and measures real audited compliance, but with no rewards, points or targets the kiosk offers little to make nurses notice it or want to try it, and the habit may fade once launch attention passes.

claude.worst_flaw: The kiosk's purpose is left vague and its records never become a validated measure. Twelve weeks of uncontrolled, small-sample monthly audits with no comparison ward can't separate any effect from the Hawthorne effect, seasonality or audit noise, and the threshold ignores the sample sizes involved.

codex.worst_flaw: All three wards receive workflow fixes, feedback and recognition together, so the pilot cannot determine whether recognition improves audited hand hygiene beyond plain feedback and workflow support.

holistic.reason: Safe, cheap, well-governed pilot with honest measurement limits and harm safeguards, but recognition with no points or prizes is low-salience for busy nurses and the kiosk benefit fades once recognition ends.

codex.worst_flaw: A rise in justified skips can trigger payouts and meet the rollout threshold while relevant article use stays flat.

claude.worst_flaw: The 70% target credits 'valid skips' and generic links through a thin 12-closure weekly QA sample with a lenient 3-of-12 pause threshold. The design never asks whether article work trades off against the CSAT bonus. Agents can therefore meet the goal with low-value skips or token links, and a sample this small cannot reliably detect that kind of displacement.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded design with QA validation, skip-gaming controls, private goals, staggered randomized waves and a pause rule, but a single hour of paid time off is a modest reward, the 70% target may feel demanding against a 12% baseline, and the prize ends after week 6 so durable change depends on the workflow becoming the default.

codex.worst_flaw: An agent can earn the reward entirely through valid “article unnecessary” entries, so payouts can rise while adoption stays flat on tickets that warrant reusable guidance.

claude.worst_flaw: The design gives no replayable event history or policy versioning and no independent shadow validation of credit, and appeals are just a flag that goes to one part-time owner, who also runs the pilot and decides on payout pauses. That makes audit and dispute handling too weak for a pay-adjacent reward.

holistic.reason: The proposal is carefully designed, with verifiable credit, an anti-gaming QA gate, a CSAT guardrail, a staggered control group and a fix-friction-first approach, but the reward is modest, the personal goal is set at only 40% of expected qualifying resolutions, and lasting change depends on the default-flow change landing.

codex.worst_flaw: The award should stay on hold because exempt tickets both earn credit and reduce the volume used to set targets, allowing agents to qualify without improving article coverage on eligible tickets.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no replayable event or policy versioning and no independent shadow validation of credit before payouts. A weekly 10-ticket QA sample is also a thin audit for a paid-time reward at 60 agents, so invalid credits could be paid out unnoticed.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes, validated credits, reachable targets, QA checks and a staggered comparison, but a one-hour reward for hitting a count could still drive box-ticking, and the lasting effect depends mainly on whether the close-flow shortcuts alone sustain the habit once the award ends.
